title: Coins in a Game Played on Two Continents
prompt: A mobile game runs in two regions, Asia and the United States. Players spend coins on items, and see which friends are online. Design how coin balances and online status behave, normally and when the link between the regions breaks.
facts: About 5,000 coin spends per second at peak; 60% of them come from players in Asia
About 95% of spends come from players in their home country's region; 5% come from players travelling abroad
A round trip between the regions takes about 150 ms; local work takes about 5 ms
A balance must never let a player spend the same coins twice; a spend must be confirmed within 300 ms; during a partition, a spend may be refused with "try again later" but never counted twice

While the regions are connected, online status may be up to 30 seconds old; during a partition, status from the other region may stay stale, and it must be up to date again within 30 seconds after the link returns
Partitions between the regions happen a few times a year and last up to 15 minutes
scope: Buying coins with real money is out of scope

requirements: States that coins need one consistent truth (no double spend), that spends may be refused during a partition, and that status may be 30 seconds old while connected, stale during a partition, and current again within 30 seconds of the link returning
estimation: Spend time across regions: 5 + 150 = 155 ms, within 300 ms

Refused spends in a 15-minute partition, for the chosen design: for example 5% × 5,000 = 250 per second × 900 s = 225,000 with a home region per player, or 40% × 5,000 = 2,000 per second × 900 s = 1.8 million with one global home in Asia
design: One place decides each player's balance (a home region per player or one global leader); status is copied between regions without waiting
data: Balance writes go through the deciding region, which checks the balance and subtracts in one step (SD 4)
Online status counted in each region and sent to the other every few seconds
tradeoffs: Names the trade-off with its condition, such as: during a partition, players whose balance lives across the break cannot spend; a single global home is simpler but refuses far more spends; choosing availability for coins would allow double spends

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, a home region per player: each player's balance lives in their home region, which checks and subtracts in one step. Travelling players (5%) wait 5 + 150 = 155 ms, within 300 ms. During a 15-minute partition only they are refused: 250 per second × 900 s = 225,000 spends, with "try again later". Online status is kept in each region and sent across every few seconds, so it is at most a few seconds old while connected; during a partition the other region's status stays stale, and the next update after the link returns, within a few seconds, brings it up to date. Trade-off: moving a player's home when they move country needs a careful handover.

Design B, one global home in Asia: all balances live in the Asian region. US players wait 5 + 150 = 155 ms per spend, within 300 ms. During a 15-minute partition all US spends are refused: 2,000 per second × 900 s = 1.8 million. Online status is kept in each region and sent across every few seconds as in Design A: stale during a partition, current again within a few seconds after it. Trade-off: simpler, with no handover between homes, but eight times as many refused spends during a partition.

assumptions: Each player has one home region
The game shows "try again later" when a spend is refused
reference.design:
Coin balances choose consistency. Each player's balance has a home region, where a spend checks the balance and subtracts in one step, so the same coins can never be spent twice.
Players at home spend in about 5 ms; the 5% travelling abroad wait about 5 + 150 = 155 ms, within 300 ms.
During a 15-minute partition, travelling players cannot reach their home region and are asked to try again later: about 250 per second × 900 s = 225,000 refused spends, and none counted twice.
Online status chooses availability: each region records its own players' status and sends it to the other region every few seconds; it is a few seconds old while connected, stays stale during a partition as the requirement allows, and the first update after the link returns, a few seconds later, brings it within 30 seconds again.
alternatives: One global home in Asia: simpler, but about 1.8 million refused spends per partition
Rejected: letting both regions accept spends from their own copy, because a player could spend the same coins on both sides during a partition

title: A Shopping List Shared by a Family
prompt: A shopping-list app lets family members add and tick items on a shared list from their phones. Families are often spread across countries, and the app runs in two regions. Design how lists stay usable and correct, normally and during a partition.
facts: About 2 million families, each making about 10 list changes a day; at peak, about 300 changes per second in total
Requirement: adding an item must always succeed, even during a partition between the regions, and no added item may be lost

While the regions are connected, other family members must see a change within 1 minute; during a partition, changes made across the break may appear only after the link returns, and must appear within 1 minute after it returns

Merge rule supplied by the team: every add creates a new entry with its own unique ID, so adding "milk" again creates a second entry; a tick records the IDs of the entries the person saw; an entry stays on the list until a tick covers its ID; a change received twice is applied once, by its ID
Each region can send and apply about 10,000 changes per second from the other region
A round trip between the regions takes about 120 ms; partitions last up to 15 minutes
scope: Accounts and sharing invitations are out of scope

requirements: States that adding must always succeed (availability), that no addition may be lost, that changes appear within 1 minute while connected, and within 1 minute after a partition ends
estimation: Average changes per second: 2 × 10⁶ × 10 = 2 × 10⁷ a day ÷ 10⁵ = 200 per second
Backlog after a 15-minute partition at the 300 per second peak: at most 300 × 900 = 270,000 changes; at 10,000 per second they are exchanged in about 27 s, within 1 minute
design: Each region accepts changes to any list from its own users and sends them to the other region without waiting; or phones keep a local copy and send changes when they can reach a region
data: Uses the supplied merge rule: entries and ticks are merged by ID, so a tick hides only the entries it saw and a concurrent re-add, with a new ID, stays
Why last write wins for the whole list would lose items
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: an item re-added during a partition stays on the list after another member ticked the old entry; family members on opposite sides see different lists until the link returns; storing every entry and tick ID costs more space than storing the list

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, both regions accept changes: each region applies its users' adds and ticks at once and sends each change to the other region within seconds, well within 1 minute. Entries and ticks are merged by ID: a tick hides only the entries it saw, a re-add has a new ID and stays, and a change received twice is applied once. About 200 changes per second on average; after a 15-minute partition at most 300 × 900 = 270,000 changes are exchanged at 10,000 per second, in about 27 s. Trade-off: an item re-added on the other side stays on the list.

Design B, a home region per list with phones that work offline: each list has a home region, and each phone keeps its own copy and a queue of its changes. A phone adds an entry with a new ID to its copy at once and sends the queue to the home region whenever it can reach it, so adding always succeeds on the phone. The home region merges entries and ticks by ID with the supplied rule. While connected, a change reaches the home region and other phones within seconds; after a 15-minute partition, at most 270,000 queued changes reach it in about 27 s at 10,000 per second. Trade-off: phones across the break keep their changes queued until the link returns.

assumptions: Phones may be offline for a while; the 1-minute limit applies to phones that are online
reference.design:
Lists choose availability. Each region accepts adds and ticks from its own users at once and sends every change to the other region within a few seconds, well inside the 1-minute limit while connected.
The list is a set of entries and a set of ticks, merged by ID with the supplied rule. A tick hides only the entries it saw; if someone ticks milk on one side while someone re-adds milk on the other, the new entry has a new ID and stays. Replaying an old change does nothing, because its ID is already known, so nothing is lost or brought back by mistake.
Load: 2 × 10⁶ × 10 ÷ 10⁵ = 200 changes per second on average. After a 15-minute partition at the 300 per second peak, at most 270,000 changes are exchanged; at 10,000 per second this takes about 27 s, within 1 minute.
alternatives: A home region per list with an offline queue on each phone: adds always succeed on the phone, synced later
Rejected: last write wins for the whole list, because two people adding different items at once would lose one of them
